The alveolus: built for diffusion

text: Thin, moist and huge, all at once.
say: Deep in your lungs are hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs. This is where the air finally meets your blood.
Oxygen moves from the air into your blood, and carbon dioxide moves the other way, by diffusion: from where there's a lot of it to where there's less.

text: Thin and moist: one cell thick.
say: The wall of each alveolus is just one cell thick, and lined with moisture for the gases to dissolve in. So the distance is tiny.

text: Huge and busy: big surface, many capillaries.
say: Together the alveoli have a huge surface area, and each one is wrapped in a dense net of capillaries that keeps carrying the oxygen away.

Carbon dioxide sets the pace

text: Your brain watches the carbon dioxide.
say: You don't have to think about breathing. Something else is keeping count.

text: More carbon dioxide: makes the blood acidic.
say: When you exercise, your muscles make more carbon dioxide, and it makes your blood more acidic.
A part of your brain called the medulla oblongata detects the change.

text: Faster and deeper: impulses to the muscles.
say: It sends impulses to your diaphragm and intercostal muscles, so you breathe faster and deeper, until the carbon dioxide is back to normal.

Carrying the gases

text: Oxygen rides on red blood cells.
say: Once the gases are in your blood, they need a ride.
Oxygen joins haemoglobin inside your red blood cells, forming oxyhaemoglobin, and is carried to every cell in your body.

text: Carbon dioxide: mostly in the plasma.
say: Carbon dioxide, made by respiration in your cells' mitochondria, travels back mostly dissolved in the plasma, as hydrogencarbonate.

text: The odd ones out: pulmonary artery and vein.
say: Usually arteries carry oxygen-rich blood. But the pulmonary artery carries blood low in oxygen to the lungs, and the pulmonary vein brings oxygen-rich blood back.

Breathing in

text: Make the chest bigger, and air rushes in.
say: Your lungs have no muscles of their own. So how do they fill with air?

text: Muscles contract: the brain sends the signal.
say: Your brain sends impulses to two sets of muscles: the diaphragm under your lungs, and the intercostal muscles between your ribs. Both contract.

text: Chest grows: diaphragm down, ribs up and out.
say: The diaphragm flattens and moves down, and the rib cage swings up and out. The space inside your chest gets bigger.

text: Air rushes in: volume up, pressure down.
say: More volume means lower pressure inside the lungs than in the air outside, so air rushes in to fill them.

text: Let the muscles go, and the air follows.
say: Breathing out, when you're resting, takes almost no effort at all. You just let go.

text: Air out: volume down, pressure up.
say: Less volume means more pressure inside the lungs than outside, so the air is pushed out.

The airway: nose to alveoli

text: Every breath takes the same route.
say: Every breath you take follows the same path, from your nose down into the depths of your lungs.

text: The nose: filters, warms and moistens.
say: In the nasal cavity, hairs and mucus filter the air, and it's warmed and moistened on its way in.

text: Throat to chest: pharynx, larynx, trachea.
say: It passes the pharynx and the larynx, your voice box, into the trachea. Rings of cartilage hold the trachea open, and the epiglottis closes over it when you swallow.

text: Into the lungs: bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli.
say: The trachea splits into two bronchi, which branch into thousands of bronchioles, ending in tiny air sacs: the alveoli. It all sits in your chest, the thoracic cavity.

Homeostasis and excretion

text: Keeping the inside of you steady.
say: This chapter is really about one big idea: keeping your insides steady.
Homeostasis means keeping your internal environment constant: the same temperature, the same water and salt, whatever is happening outside.
Excretion is getting rid of waste made by your own cells, like urea and carbon dioxide.
Don't mix it up with egestion. That's just getting rid of food you never digested.

Filtration: squeezing the blood

text: High pressure pushes small molecules out.
say: It all starts with a squeeze.

text: Narrow exit: efferent narrower than afferent.
say: Blood comes into the glomerulus through a wide vessel, the afferent arteriole, and leaves through a narrower one, the efferent arteriole. That squeeze builds up pressure.

text: Pushed out: water, glucose, salts, urea.

text: Too big: cells and proteins stay.

text: Your brain decides how much water to keep.
say: Your kidneys don't decide on their own how much water to keep. Your brain turns the dial.

text: Short of water: the hypothalamus notices.

text: More ADH: from the pituitary gland.

Inside a kidney

text: Three zones, each with a job.
say: Cut a kidney in half, and you can see three different zones.
The outer layer is the cortex. That's where the filtering happens, in about a million tiny tubes called nephrons.
Inside is the medulla, made of cone-shaped pyramids. The long loops of the nephrons dip down here to save water.
In the middle is the pelvis, a funnel that collects the urine and pours it into the ureter.

The general defence system
Before your immune system even notices an invader, it has to get past your general defences.
Your skin is a tough barrier. Mucus traps microbes, cilia sweep them away, and acid in your stomach kills most of what you swallow.
Any pathogen that gets through meets the phagocytes, like monocytes and macrophages. They engulf it, and digest it with enzymes.

text: Not specific: the same for every invader.
say: These defences treat every invader the same way, and they're always ready. That's why this is called the general, or innate, system.

Testing a new vaccine

text: A fair test, on a lot of people.
say: Before a new vaccine is used, it has to be tested very carefully. Here's how scientists make that test fair.

text: A control group: gets a placebo.
say: Half the volunteers get the vaccine. The other half, the control group, get a placebo: a harmless injection with no vaccine in it, so the two groups can be compared fairly.
Tens of thousands of people, from many countries, take part. A large, varied sample makes the results more reliable, and true for everyone.

text: Only who was tested: no further than the data.
say: And the conclusion can only cover the people who were tested. If no children took part, we can't say it works for children.

Pathogens: what makes us ill
A pathogen is anything that causes disease. And they come in surprisingly different shapes and sizes.

text: Many kinds: bacteria, viruses, fungi and more.
say: Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists like the one that causes malaria, and even parasitic worms.
The oddest are prions: proteins folded into the wrong shape. They cause brain diseases like BSE and CJD, with no cells and no genes at all.

text: Foreign markers: antigens give them away.
say: Every pathogen carries molecules on its surface that your body doesn't recognise. These antigens are how your immune system knows something is wrong.

How a virus multiplies

text: It hijacks your cells to make copies of itself.
say: A virus can't make anything by itself. So it borrows a cell, and takes it over.

text: Attach and enter: its nucleic acid gets in.
say: First, the virus attaches to a host cell, and its DNA or RNA gets inside.

text: Copies: made by the host cell.
say: Then the host cell's own ribosomes, enzymes and energy are used to copy the viral genes and make new protein coats.

text: Assembled and released: the cell often bursts.
say: The parts are assembled into hundreds of new viruses, which burst out of the cell to infect the next one.

B and T lymphocytes

text: The specific defence system's special forces.
say: Lymphocytes are the specialists of your immune system. Each one is trained to recognise just one antigen.
Lymphocytes are made in the bone marrow. B lymphocytes make antibodies against the antigens they recognise.

text: T cells: helper, killer, suppressor, memory.
say: Helper T cells recognise antigens and switch the other lymphocytes on. Killer T cells find infected cells and burst them with a chemical called perforin.

text: Off, and remember: suppressor and memory cells.
say: Suppressor T cells switch the attack off when it's over. Memory cells stay for years, ready for the next time.
Antibiotics and resistance

text: Powerful against bacteria, useless against viruses.
say: Antibiotics are one of medicine's greatest discoveries. But bacteria are fighting back.

text: Antibiotics: made by microbes, kill bacteria.
say: An antibiotic is a substance made by a micro-organism, like penicillin from a fungus, that kills bacteria or stops them growing.

text: Not viruses: no effect on them at all.
say: They have no effect on viruses. So antibiotics won't cure a cold, the flu or COVID-19.
When antibiotics are overused, a few bacteria with resistance genes survive and multiply. Soon the whole population is resistant, and the antibiotic stops working.

What is a virus?

text: Genes in a protein shell, and not quite alive.
say: A virus is one of the strangest things in biology. It's not even made of cells.

text: Two parts: nucleic acid in a protein coat.
say: Every virus has just two main parts: its genes, made of DNA or RNA, packed inside a coat of protein called the capsid.

text: No cells: so is it living?
say: It has no cells, no organelles and no metabolism of its own. That's why biologists find it so hard to call a virus living.

text: Obligate parasite: it needs a host cell.
say: A virus can only reproduce inside a living host cell. On its own, it simply waits. That makes it an obligate parasite.

Vaccination and immunity

text: Meeting the enemy safely, ahead of time.
say: What if your body could practise fighting a disease, without ever getting sick? That's exactly what a vaccine does.

text: Harmless dose: a weakened or dead pathogen.
say: A vaccine is a harmless form of a pathogen, weakened, dead, or just its antigens, put into the body.

text: Active immunity: your own antibodies and memory cells.
say: Your body makes its own antibodies and memory cells against it. That's active immunity, and it can last for years.
Passive immunity is when you're given ready-made antibodies, from an injection, or from breast milk. It works straight away, but fades within weeks.

How diseases spread

text: A pathogen needs to reach new hosts.
say: For a disease to spread, the pathogen has to keep finding new people to infect.

text: Getting about: travel, touch, water, mosquitoes.
say: Pathogens spread through the air, through touch, food and water, or carried by animals like mosquitoes, and travel takes them around the world.

text: No immunity: and it spreads fast.
say: In a population with no immunity, like the rabbits hit by myxomatosis, or people who haven't been vaccinated, a disease can spread very quickly.

text: Immunity builds: and the death rate falls.
say: Over time the survivors, and their offspring, can be immune, so the disease kills fewer of them.

Antigens and antibodies

text: A lock, and the key made to fit it.
say: Your specific defences work a bit like a lock and a key.
An antigen is a foreign molecule, usually a protein on the surface of a pathogen, that makes your body produce antibodies.

text: Antibody: a protein made to fit it.
say: An antibody is a Y-shaped protein, made by B lymphocytes, with a shape that fits one antigen, and only that one.
When antibodies lock onto antigens, the pathogens clump together and are marked, so phagocytes can find them and destroy them.

Harmful and helpful viruses

text: Most cause disease, but some are useful.
say: Viruses are famous for making us ill. But some of them are surprisingly useful.
Viruses cause the common cold, flu, measles, COVID-19 and AIDS in people, and diseases like tobacco mosaic in plants.
But scientists can use them to carry useful genes into cells. That's genetic engineering, with the virus as the vector.
Some viruses, called bacteriophages, attack only bacteria. They could be used to treat infections that antibiotics can no longer cure.
